parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Look at what the voltmeter is actually measuring. It is connected across the 3400 ohm resistor plus the thermistor, so its 6.0 V is only part of the 9.6 V e.m.f. Think about what is left for the 5800 ohm resistor.
Hint 2: Once you have the potential difference across just the 5800 ohm resistor, link p.d., current and resistance for that one component and rearrange to find the current.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the voltage left for the top resistor**
In a series loop the e.m.f. is shared between all the components. Here the voltmeter reads $6.0 \, \text{V}$ across the bottom branch containing the $3400 \, \Omega$ resistor and the thermistor together. That leaves the rest of the $9.6 \, \text{V}$ for the $5800 \, \Omega$ resistor: $$V_{5800} = 9.6 - 6.0 = 3.6 \, \text{V}$$

Step 2: **Apply Ohm's law to the 5800 ohm resistor**
For any resistor $V = IR$. Rearranged for current: $$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{3.6}{5800}$$ $$I = 6.2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{A}$$ This is the series current, so it is the same everywhere in the loop.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Remember current is the same at every point in a series circuit, so the current you just found in the 5800 ohm resistor also flows through the 3400 ohm resistor and the thermistor.

Hint 2: The voltmeter reading of 6.0 V is the p.d. across those two lower components in series. Use this voltage and the common current to find their total resistance, then subtract the known 3400 ohm.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the common series current**
Let the thermistor resistance be $R$. The $3400 \, \Omega$ resistor and thermistor are in series, so their combined resistance is $3400 + R$ and they carry the same current $I = 6.2 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{A}$ as the top resistor. Their combined p.d. is the voltmeter reading: $$6.0 = I \times (3400 + R)$$

Step 2: **Solve for the thermistor resistance**
$$3400 + R = \frac{6.0}{6.2 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 9680 \, \Omega$$ $$R \approx 9680 - 3400 \approx 6.3 \times 10^{3} \, \Omega$$

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: e.m.f. as energy per unit charge E = W/Q
hints: Hint 1: Think about what e.m.f. means in joules per coulomb. Each coulomb that moves through the battery carries away a fixed amount of stored chemical energy.
Hint 2: Calculate the energy delivered by the battery for 330 C, then subtract this used energy from the initial $2.6 \times 10^{4}$ J to leave the final stored energy.
parts.proper_answer: Energy delivered $= EQ = 9.6 \times 330 = 3170 \, \text{J}$. Final stored energy $= 2.6 \times 10^{4} - 3170 = 2.3 \times 10^{4} \, \text{J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Calculate energy transferred by the moving charge**
E.m.f. is energy transferred per unit charge, $E = W/Q$. So for charge $Q$ passing: $$W = E Q = 9.6 \times 330 \approx 3170 \, \text{J}$$ This is the chemical energy converted to electrical energy.

Step 2: **Subtract from the initial store**
$$\text{final energy} = \text{initial energy} - \text{energy used}$$ $$= 2.6 \times 10^{4} - 3170 \approx 2.3 \times 10^{4} \, \text{J}$$

parts.label: (d)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how a standard NTC thermistor responds to temperature - its resistance falls when it gets hot because more charge carriers are freed, so work backwards from a rise in resistance.
parts.proper_answer: decrease. Resistance of NTC thermistor increases when temperature falls.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link resistance to temperature for an NTC thermistor**
A thermistor in this type of circuit is NTC, negative temperature coefficient. Heating it gives more mobile electrons and lower resistance. So if resistance has gone up, the opposite has happened and the temperature must have decreased.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
key_concepts: Ohm's law for whole circuit I = E/R_total
hints: Hint 1: Think about the total resistance of the whole series loop when the thermistor resistance grows, and what that does to the single loop current driven by the fixed 9.6 V e.m.f.
parts.proper_answer: decrease. Total resistance increases so for constant e.m.f. current $I = E/R_{total}$ falls.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See the effect on total resistance and current**
Total resistance is $5800 + 3400 + R_{therm}$. If $R_{therm}$ increases, $R_{total}$ increases. With $E$ fixed and negligible internal resistance: $$I = \frac{E}{R_{total}}$$ so the current in the whole series circuit, including the thermistor, decreases.

parts.label: (d)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think of the circuit as a potential divider - the component whose resistance grows takes a larger share of the fixed 9.6 V, even though the current falls a little.
parts.proper_answer: increase. Thermistor takes a larger proportion of the e.m.f. as its resistance forms a larger fraction of total resistance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply the potential divider idea**
The p.d. across the thermistor is $V = I \times R_{therm}$. Although $I$ falls, $R_{therm}$ has risen by a larger factor, so its share $R_{therm}/R_{total}$ of the 9.6 V grows. Another way to see it is that the p.d. across the fixed $5800 \, \Omega$ resistor $IR$ must fall because $I$ falls, leaving more of the 9.6 V for the lower branch and in particular for the thermistor. So $V_{therm}$ increases.
